Alexander Bortnikov (born 15 November 1951) is a Russian intelligence officer who has served as the director of the Federal Security Service (FSB) since 2008.

Andy Beshear (b-SHEER; born November 29, 1977) is an American politician and attorney serving since 2019 as the 63rd governor of Kentucky.

Aung San (13 February 1915 - 19 July 1947) was a Burmese politician, independence activist and revolutionary.

Wage labor, capital accumulation, commodification, and an emphasis on innovation are the hallmarks of which profit-driven economic system?
Capitalism is an economic system based on the private ownership of the means of production and its use for the purpose of obtaining profit.

Daughter of the sun god Helios, this Greek mythological witch famously turned Odysseus's crew into animals using her mastery of potions and a magic wand during his journey home from Troy — who is she?
Circe (Ancient) is a witch, sometimes considered a goddess or a nymph.

Dean Corll (December 24, 1939 - August 8, 1973) was an American serial killer and sex offender who abducted, raped, tortured and murdered at least 29 teenage boys and young men between 1970 and 1973 in Houston and Pasadena, Texas.

Egalitarianism (from French gal 'equal'; also equalitarianism) is a school of thought within political philosophy that builds on the concept of social equality, prioritizing it for all people.

Though this exact phrase never appears in Abrahamic scripture, it describes beings cast out of Heaven for sins like pride or lust, often blamed for corrupting humanity with forbidden knowledge — what are they called?
Fallen angel are angels who were expelled from Heaven.

Garry Kasparov (born Garik Kimovich Weinstein on 13 April 1963) is a Russian chess grandmaster, political activist and writer, who was the World Chess Champion from 1985 to 2000.
Catherine the Great's lover, favorite, and possibly her consort, this Russian statesman died during the negotiations that ended his war with the Ottomans — who was he?
Grigory Potemkin was Russian military leader and statesman (1739–1791).
House speaker, secretary of state, and a three-time loser of the presidency, this Kentuckian earned the nickname 'the Great Compromiser' for defusing sectional crises — who was he?
Henry Clay (April 12, 1777 - June 29, 1852) was an American lawyer, statesman, and diplomat who represented Kentucky in both the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate.

A Scottish politician born to Pakistani immigrant parents became the youngest justice secretary in 2018, then health secretary, before leading his party and nation from March 2023 to May 2024. Who served as First Minister of Scotland?
Humza Yousaf (born 7 April 1985) is a Scottish politician who served as First Minister of Scotland and Leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP) from March 2023 to May 2024.
Twin brother of Esau, this Torah patriarch tricked his aging father into giving him the blessing meant for his sibling, after already buying that sibling's birthright — who is he?
Jacob is the third Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions.

Jim Jordan (born February 17, 1964) is an American politician who has served in the U.S.
This member of the First Triumvirate led the Gallic Wars, defeated Pompey, and sparked the political chaos that would end the Republic. Who?

Julius Caesar (12 or 13 July 100 BC - 15 March 44 BC) was a Roman general, statesman, and author who was the dictator of the Roman Republic almost continuously from 49 BC until his assassination in 44 BC.
Though named for one region, this Hohenzollern realm was actually based in the Margraviate of Brandenburg and rose from the work of 'The Great Elector.' What was it?
Kingdom of Prussia was a German state that existed from 1701 to 1918.
Born in Karnal to a wealthy Rajput family, this lawyer became the first prime minister of his newly founded nation and, revered as 'Leader of the Nation,' was assassinated in 1951 — who was he?
Liaquat Ali Khan (1 October 1895 - 16 October 1951) was a Pakistani lawyer, politician and statesman who served as the first prime minister of Pakistan from 1947 until his assassination in 1951.
The first Filipino to head a government of the entire Philippines, this president defeated Emilio Aguinaldo in 1935 and has a Metro Manila city named after him — who was he?

Manuel L. Quezon (19 August 1878 - 1 August 1944), also known by his initials MLQ, was a Filipino lawyer, statesman, soldier, and politician who served as the second president of the Philippines from 1935 until his death in 1944.

This Turkish politician and economist has served as Minister of Treasury and Finance since 2023, having previously been both deputy prime minister and finance minister under two different Turkish prime ministers — who is he?
Mehmet Şimşek (born 1 January 1967) is a Turkish politician and economist, who has been serving as the Minister of Treasury and Finance since 4 June 2023.
Before leading Iraq's government from 2022, this politician held an unusually long list of 'acting minister' titles, including trade, finance, and migration. Who is he?
Mohammed Shia' al-Sudani (born 4 March 1970) is an Iraqi politician and former agricultural engineer who served as the prime minister of Iraq from 2022 to 2026.

Formed in the wake of Greece's military junta collapsing in 1974, this liberal-conservative party has been one of the country's two dominant political forces for decades, long rivaling the Panhellenic Socialist Movement — what is it?

New Democracy (Greece) is a liberal-conservative political party in Greece. New Democracy and PASOK were created in the wake of the toppling of the military junta in 1974, ruling Greece in succession for the next four decades.
Born Kathleen Ruska and once known as Kath Walker, she became the first Aboriginal Australian to publish a book of verse while campaigning for Aboriginal rights. Who was she?

Oodgeroo Noonuccal (born Kathleen Jean Mary Ruska; 3 November 1920 - 16 September 1993), earlier known as Kath Walker, was an Aboriginal Australian political activist, artist and educator, who campaigned for Aboriginal rights.
This Confucian scholar-turned-revolutionary led rebel armies against French colonial forces in 19th-century Vietnam, refusing to surrender even after they desecrated his ancestral tombs. Who was he?
Phan Đình Phùng (1847 - January 21, 1896) was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led rebel armies against French colonial forces in Vietnam.
A businessman who became Lebanon's wealthiest politician, he helped forge the Taif Agreement ending the civil war and led the rebuilding of Beirut before his 2005 assassination — who was he?
Rafic Hariri (1 November 1944 - 14 February 2005) was a Lebanese businessman and politician who served as prime minister of Lebanon from 1992 to 1998 and again from 2000 to 2004.
The first Philippine president from Mindanao and the oldest to take office at 71, he had earlier served three non-consecutive terms as mayor of Davao City. Who is he?
Rodrigo Duterte (born March 28, 1945) is a Filipino politician who served as the 16th president of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022.
Originally known by a different name before it was changed, this biblical matriarch was the wife of Abraham and mother of Isaac, revered across Judaism, Christianity, and Islam — who is she?
Sarah (originally Sarai) is a biblical matriarch, prophet, and major figure in Abrahamic religions.

United Arab Republic was a country and sovereign state in the Middle East from 1958 to 1971.

War in Afghanistan (2001–2021) was a prolonged armed conflict lasting from 2001 to 2021.

Yoav Gallant (born 8 November 1958) is an Israeli politician and former military officer who served as minister of defense between 2022 and 2024.

Abdul Hamid II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1876 to 1909.

Ahmet Davutoğlu: Prime Minister of Turkey from 2014 to 2016. The AKP lost its parliamentary majority in the June 2015 general election, though it remained the largest party.

Ariel Sharon: Prime Minister of Israel from 2001 to 2006.

Aztecs: Ethnic group of central Mexico and its civilization.

Daniel arap Moi: President of Kenya from 1978 to 2002.

Ding Xuexiang: First-ranking Vice Premier of China since 2023.

Edmund Ironside: King of England in 1016. Edmund's reign was spent fighting against a Danish invasion led by Cnut.

End of World War II in Europe

False Dmitry I: Tsar of Russia from 1605 to 1606.
A longtime aide to Gerhard Schröder before serving as Germany's top diplomat twice, he has been President of Germany since 2017 — who is he?

Frank-Walter Steinmeier: President of Germany since 2017. Frank-Walter Steinmeier (German: [ˈfʁaŋkˌvaltɐ ˈʃtaɪnˌmaɪ.ɐ]; born 5 January 1956) is a German politician who has served as President of Germany since 2017.
Born in Rostock and later a Prussian field marshal, this military leader helped defeat Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and again at Waterloo in 1815 — who is he?
Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher: Prussian field marshal (1742–1819)
According to Exodus, the Israelites made this idol of a young bovine while Moses was away on Mount Sinai — what was it?
Golden calf: Idol in the Torah, the Bible, and the Quran.
He became the fifteenth ruler of an Arabian dynasty in 2020 after his cousin's death, having previously served for decades as Minister of Heritage and Culture — who is he?
Haitham bin Tariq: Sultan of Oman since 2020.

Said to be the most beautiful woman in the world and a daughter of Zeus, her elopement with a foreign prince triggered a legendary decade-long war after her first husband, the Spartan king, lost her — who was she?
Helen of Troy: Most beautiful woman in Greek mythology.
Owned by Cover Corporation, this virtual YouTuber talent agency manages dozens of streamers across three languages with a combined 80 million-plus subscribers — what is it?
Hololive Production: Japanese virtual YouTuber agency. In December 2019, Hololive was merged with Cover's male Holostars agency and INoNaKa music label under the unified "Hololive Production" brand.
A young military officer with a geology degree from Ouagadougou, he seized power as interim president of Burkina Faso after a 2022 coup, championing pan-Africanist and anti-Western views. Who is he?
Ibrahim Traoré: Leader of Burkina Faso since 2022.

Formed in 1946 by former supporters of Benito Mussolini's Republican Fascist Party, which political party became postwar Italy's fourth-largest by the early 1960s while presenting itself as the defender of fascism's legacy?
Italian Social Movement: Neo-fascist political party, 1946–1955.

Janata Dal (United): Political party in India.

Born under a cloud of doubt about his parentage after his mother's captivity by a rival tribe, this early Mongol Empire prince became a military commander and the ancestor of the rulers of the Golden Horde — who is he?
Jochi: Mongol prince and general (c. 1182 – c. 1225)
Publishing a new scripture at age 24, this American founder of a major religious movement drew tens of thousands of followers before his death just fourteen years later — who was he?
Joseph Smith: Founder of the Latter Day Saint movement (1805–1844)

Karel Schwarzenberg: Czech politician and noble (1937–2023)

Kingdom of Bohemia: Monarchy in Central Europe (1198–1918)
This Guinean general seized power in a 1984 coup and then ruled the West African nation as its second president until his death in 2008 — who was he?
Lansana Conté: President of Guinea from 1984 to 2008.

Marcos Pérez Jiménez: Dictator of Venezuela from 1952 to 1958. The economy of Venezuela developed rapidly while Pérez was in power.
This US Army general led the 82nd Airborne in Sicily, Italy and Normandy, later commanded a corps at the Battle of the Bulge, and went on to be Supreme Allied Commander Europe — who was he?
Matthew Ridgway: United States Army general (1895–1993)
A Catholic priest revered as the Father of the Nation, he delivered the famous 'Cry of Dolores' on 16 September 1810 to launch Mexico's independence movement — who is he?
Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla: Mexican Catholic preacher (1753–1811)
Born in Mashhad and the second son of Iran's second supreme leader, this cleric commanded the Basij militia from 2009 and became his country's third supreme leader in 2026 — who is he?

Mojtaba Khamenei: Supreme Leader of Iran since 2026. Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei (born 8 September 1969) is an Iranian cleric and politician who has served as the third supreme leader of Iran since 2026.

Crowned King of Rome at birth and later nicknamed 'the Eaglet,' he was the disputed Emperor of the French for all of two weeks in 1815 before living out his days in Vienna — which son of a famous conqueror?
Napoleon II: Disputed Emperor of the French in 1815 (1811–1832)
Shared across Jainism, Hinduism, Buddhism, and Sikhism, this state of liberation marks the end of the cycle of rebirth and the extinguishing of worldly passions — what is it?
Nirvana: Liberation from repeated rebirth in saṃsāra.
Having joined the Italian resistance as a teenager in World War II, this journalist grew famous for fierce interviews with the likes of Henry Kissinger, Golda Meir, and the Shah of Iran — who is she?
Oriana Fallaci: Italian journalist and author (1929–2006)

This semi-nomadic Turkic people controlled the steppes of southeastern Europe and Crimea in the 9th and 10th centuries, waging war against the early Rus' state for over two hundred years — who were they?
Pechenegs: Extinct Turkic people. The Pechenegs or Patzinaks, were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who spoke the Pecheneg language.
Serving as the 64th Bishop of Rome from 590 until 604, this former Roman prefect sent missionaries to England, including Augustine of Canterbury — who was he?
Pope Gregory I: 64th Bishop of Rome; head of the Roman Catholic Church from AD 590 to 604.

Founded in 1891 by Leandro N. Alem, this Argentine political party is the country's second-oldest active party and a longtime human-rights advocate that has been banned under military rule — which party?
Radical Civic Union: Political party in Argentina. The Radical Civic Union (Spanish: Unión Cívica Radical, UCR) is a major political party in Argentina.
Known by the abbreviation PRO and led by former Argentine president Mauricio Macri, which party has governed Buenos Aires since 2007?
Republican Proposal: Political party in Argentina.
Born in Hong Kong and educated at Eton, this British former diplomat and MP walked solo across Asia after leaving the Foreign Office, and now co-hosts a podcast with Alastair Campbell — who is he?

Stefano Bandecchi: Italian politician and entrepreneur. Stefano Bandecchi (born 4 April 1961) is an Italian politician and entrepreneur.
Reigning over the Georgian Golden Age from 1184 to 1213, this Bagrationi monarch was the first woman to rule Georgia in her own right and was given the title 'King' in medieval sources — who was she?
Tamar I: Queen of Georgia from 1184 to 1213. Tamar was successful in neutralizing this opposition and embarked on an energetic foreign policy aided by the decline of the hostile Seljuk Turks.

This South Australian premier governed for over 26 years — the longest unbroken stretch of any elected leader in Australian history — and was famous for shamelessly haranguing federal leaders into funding his state. Who was he?
Thomas Playford IV: 20th-century Australian politician and fruit grower (1896–1981)
This Indian politician served as Maharashtra's 19th chief minister from 2019 to 2022 while also editing a newspaper for over a decade — who is he?
Uddhav Thackeray: 19th Chief Minister of Maharashtra from 2019 to 2022 (born 1960)
In 1976, this Soviet pilot defected to the West by flying his MiG-25 'Foxbat' jet interceptor to Japan, handing the CIA what George H. W. Bush called an 'intelligence bonanza' — who is he?

Beginning with the 1916 death of Yuan Shikai, this chaotic decade-plus in Chinese history saw the country splinter under rival military cliques until Sun Yat-sen's Nationalists challenged the Beijing government for legitimacy — which period?
Warlord Era: Period in the history of the Republic of China (1916–1928)
First achieved in Australasia before spreading to Europe and the Americas, this democratic right for female voters began its 'first wave' in 1893 in English-speaking countries — what right?
Women's suffrage: Legal right of women to vote.
A close associate of Gandhi and a founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, this Berlin-educated educationist rose to become president of India, dying in office in 1969 — who was he?
Zakir Husain: President of India from 1967 to 1969.
Which of these people was born first?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?

Omar Khayyam (born 1048) is the earliest of the four. Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) was a Persian poet and polymath, known for his contributions to mathematics, astronomy, philosophy, and Persian literature.
Who among these was born first?
Havelock Ellis (born 1859) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Assembly language (founded 1949) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is an astronomer?
Who among these is a mathematician?
Leonhard Euler is a mathematician. Euler has been called a "universal genius" who "was fully equipped with almost unlimited powers of imagination, intellectual gifts and extraordinary memory".
Pick the chemist from these four.
Maud Menten is a chemist. Maud Leonora Menten (March 20, 1879 – July 17, 1960) was a Canadian physician and chemist.
What is the atomic number of Silicon?
Silicon (SILL-ih-kən) is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
In what year was Max Born?
Max Born: During World War I, Born was originally placed as a radio operator, but his specialist knowledge led to his being moved to research duties on sound ranging.
In what year was Fermat's Last Theorem discovered?
Fermat's Last Theorem: The proposition was first stated as a theorem by Pierre de Fermat around 1637 in the margin of a copy of Arithmetica.
In what year was Selenium discovered?
Selenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Se and atomic number 34.
Metoprolol: Pfizer. It is also used to prevent further heart problems after myocardial infarction and to prevent headaches in those with migraines.
In which country is Douglas A-4 Skyhawk based?
Douglas A-4 Skyhawk: United States. It was originally designated A4D under the United States Navy's pre-1962 designation system.
Who is credited with discovering Xenon?
Xenon: William Ramsay. Xenon is a chemical element; it has symbol Xe and atomic number 54.
Who is credited with discovering RDX?
RDX: Georg Friedrich Henning. RDX (Research Department Explosive or Royal Demolition Explosive), or hexogen, also known by other names, is an organic compound with the formula (CH2N2O2)3.
Who is credited with discovering Aluminium?
Aluminium: Hans Christian Ørsted. Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13.
This tall wetland monocot, also known as muskrat root, may be toxic if ingested and has no proven clinical benefit despite traditional medicinal use — which plant?
Acorus calamus (also called sweet flag, sway or muskrat root, among many other common names) is a species of flowering plant with psychoactive chemicals.
Often caused by misaligned or unevenly focused eyes in early childhood, this is the most common cause of single-eye vision loss in kids and young adults, nicknamed 'lazy eye' — what condition is it?
Amblyopia is a disorder of sight in which the brain fails to fully process input from one eye and over time favors the other eye.
Known as 'doodlebugs' for the trails they leave in sand, these insect larvae dig pits to ambush wandering ants, while the winged adults are often mistaken for dragonflies — what are they?
Antlion are a group of about 2,000 species of insect in the neuropteran family Myrmeleontidae.
Caused by poor circulation, lost nerve supply, or simple disuse, this process shrinks a cell, organ, or tissue below its normal mature size — what's it called?
Atrophy is the partial or complete wasting away of a part of the body.
Coined in 1814 by chemist William Hyde Wollaston, this polyatomic anion forms as carbonic acid loses a proton, and plays a crucial role buffering the body's pH — what's the ion?
Bicarbonate (American; nomenclature: hydrogencarbonate) is an intermediate form in the deprotonation of carbonic acid.
Located in the head in most animals with nervous systems, this organ receives sensory information, generates thought and cognition, and coordinates the body's muscles and glands — name the organ?
Brain is an organ that serves as the center of the nervous system in all vertebrate and most invertebrate animals.
This Italian mastiff breed once hunted big game and herded cattle, and today mostly serves as a guard dog and loyal companion — name the breed?
Cane Corso is an Italian breed of mastiff. It is usually kept as a companion dog or guard dog; it may also be used to protect livestock.
Famous for color-shifting camouflage and zygodactylous, pincer-like feet, which family of roughly 200 Old World lizard species is this?
Chameleon (family Chamaeleonidae) are a distinctive and highly specialized clade of Old World lizards with 200 species described as of June 2015.
Living in a symbiotic partnership with sea anemones that shelter them from predators, these Indo-Pacific reef fish live in groups led by a dominant breeding female. What fish are they?
Clownfish (genus Amphiprion) are saltwater fish found in the warm and tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific.

This cosmopolitan bird family includes crows, ravens, magpies, and jays, and its roughly 135 species are known for remarkable intelligence, including self-awareness demonstrated in mirror tests — what's the family?
Corvidae is a cosmopolitan family of oscine passerine birds that contains the crows, ravens, rooks, magpies, jackdaws, jays, treepies, choughs, and nutcrackers.
Often called eczema, this umbrella term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness, and a rash, sometimes with small blisters or thickened skin — what is it?
Dermatitis is a term used for different types of skin inflammation, typically characterized by itchiness, redness and a rash.
Sometimes triggered by lead poisoning or reactions to neuroleptic drugs, this neurological disorder produces involuntary, twisting muscle contractions — what is it?

Dystonia is a neurological hyperkinetic movement disorder in which sustained or repetitive muscle contractions occur involuntarily, resulting in twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal fixed postures.
Also known as human herpesvirus 4, this common virus was the first identified oncogenic virus and causes infectious mononucleosis in 90% of cases. What is it?
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is one of the nine known human herpesvirus types in the herpes family, and is one of the most common viruses in humans.
This intracellular protein buffers the body against both iron deficiency and iron overload, and small amounts leak into the blood where doctors measure it as a diagnostic marker — what protein is it?
Ferritin is a universal intracellular and extracellular protein that stores iron and releases it in a controlled fashion.
Reclassified twice before settling into its own genus, this Gram-variable, non-spore-forming coccobacillus is barely one to 1.5 micrometers across — which species?
Gardnerella vaginalis is a species of Gram-variable-staining facultative anaerobic bacteria.
This applied art and academic discipline uses text and images to craft visual communications aimed at specific audiences and objectives — what field is it?
Graphic design is a profession, academic discipline and applied art that involves creating visual communications intended to transmit specific messages to social groups, with specific objectives.
Credited with putting middle-class Americans behind the wheel, this industrialist lent his surname to the very philosophy of assembly-line manufacturing. Who is he?
Henry Ford (July 30, 1863 - April 7, 1947) was an American industrialist and business magnate.
This endocrine condition floods the body with thyroid hormone, causing a racing heart, heat intolerance, tremor, and weight loss — and a rare 'storm' can be deadly; what is it?
Hyperthyroidism is a endocrine disease in which the thyroid gland produces excessive amounts of thyroid hormones.

A colorless, flammable organic compound with a pungent odor, this liquid is miscible in water, ethanol, and chloroform, and is widely used as a solvent and disinfectant. It's commonly abbreviated as IPA—what is it?
Isopropyl alcohol (IUPAC name propan-2-ol and also called isopropanol or 2-propanol, commonly abbreviated as IPA) is a colorless, flammable, organic compound with a pungent odor.
This American social psychologist built 'moral foundations theory' on the idea that our moral reasoning springs from innate gut feelings rather than logic — who is he?
Jonathan Haidt (HYTE; born October 19, 1963) is an American social psychologist and author.
Originally a water-retrieving gun dog from Italy's Po Delta marshes, this breed later became prized for hunting truffles once its wetland habitat was drained — what breed is it?
Lagotto Romagnolo is an Italian breed of dog.

The second woman to earn a physics doctorate from the University of Vienna, this Austrian-Swedish scientist became the first female full physics professor in Germany — and was instrumental in discovering nuclear fission. Who is she?
Lise Meitner (7 November 1878 - 27 October 1968) was an Austrian and Swedish nuclear physicist who was instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission.

Made by every living organism and responsible for much of the sour taste in fruit, this dicarboxylic food additive's salt form also serves as a key intermediate in the cell's central metabolic energy cycle — what compound is it?
Malic acid is an organic compound with the molecular formula HO2CCH(OH)CH2CO2H.

This mammal family, uniting skunks and stink badgers, is defined by highly developed scent glands used to ward off predators, and was only split from the weasel family in the 1990s — what family is it?
Mephitidae is a family of mammals comprising the skunks and stink badgers.
In 1812 Étienne Geoffroy grouped the apes with the Cercopithecidae under the name Catarrhini, or "Old World" members of this familiar simian group — what common name is it?
Monkey is a common name that may refer to most mammals of the infraorder Simiiformes, also known as simians.
This silvery lanthanide, found in the minerals monazite and bastnäsite, is about as common as cobalt or nickel despite its 'rare earth' label — which element?
Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz, and named his improved early radio receiver the 'coherer' — whose key 'syntonic' tuning patents helped birth radio?
Oliver Lodge (12 June 1851 - 22 August 1940) was an English physicist and electrical engineer whose investigations into electromagnetic radiation (EMR) contributed to the development of radio.
This galliform game bird, native to Europe, Asia, and Africa, was once lumped in with pheasants and quail, but DNA suggests it isn't one distinct group at all — which bird is it?
Partridge is a medium-sized galliform bird in any of several genera, with a wide native distribution throughout parts of Europe, Asia and Africa.

Sitting at the intersection of textual criticism, literary criticism, history, and linguistics, this scholarly discipline studies language through oral and written historical sources — what is it called?
Philology (from Ancient Greek (philologa) 'love of word') is the study of language in oral and written historical sources.

This category of polymers, most commonly known in the form of PET, is prized for clothing but — unlike some of its naturally occurring plant and insect cousins — rarely biodegrades — what material is it?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.

Harvested from the seeds of several Plantago species, this common dietary fiber supplement relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and occasionally doubles as a food thickener — what is it called?
Psyllium is the common name used for several members of the plant genus Plantago whose seeds are used commercially for the production of mucilage.
Derived from an Ancient Greek word for 'flow,' this umbrella term covers more than 200 different conditions causing chronic joint or connective-tissue pain, including arthritis — what's the term?
Rheumatism (from the Ancient Greek, rhema) or rheumatic disorders are conditions causing chronic, often intermittent pain affecting the joints or connective tissue.
Which genus of 20 to 30 species of flowering plants in the family Adoxaceae produces both a fragrant white flower cluster and a dark berry, each with their own distinct common name?

Sambucus is a genus of between 20 and 30 species of flowering plants in the family Adoxaceae. The various species are commonly referred to as elder, with the flowers as elderflower, and the fruit as elderberry.

Though many are crustaceans more closely related to insects than to fish, which group of exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates, including molluscs and echinoderms, is a leading cause of food allergies?
Shellfish are exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates used as food, including various species of molluscs, crustaceans, and echinoderms.
This leafy green vegetable's high oxalate content gives raw and cooked versions noticeably different flavors, with blanching helping to tone it down — what vegetable is it?
Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) is a leafy green flowering plant native to Central and Western Asia.
This South African biologist established the tiny roundworm C. elegans as a model organism, work that helped earn him a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Who was he?
Sydney Brenner (13 January 1927 - 5 April 2019) was a South African biologist.
A European Space Agency astronaut who is also a musician and writer, this Frenchman logged two six-month stints aboard the ISS, the second launched via SpaceX Crew Dragon in 2021 — who is he?
Thomas Pesquet (French; born 27 February 1978, is a French aerospace engineer, pilot, European Space Agency astronaut, actor, musician, and writer.
Built in the Soviet Union from 1966 to 1989 for short-haul routes, this narrow-body jet earned the NATO codename 'Crusty' — which airliner is it?
Tupolev Tu-134 (NATO reporting name: Crusty) is a twin-engined, narrow-body jet airliner built in the Soviet Union for short and medium-haul routes from 1966 to 1989.
This canid genus contains the 'true foxes' — smaller and bushier-tailed than any wolf or jackal, typically living two to four years, occasionally a decade — which genus?
Vulpes is a genus of the subfamily Caninae.
Each individual's coat is unique, and the best evidence suggests their black-and-white pattern wards off biting flies — which striped African equine is this?
Zebra (subgenus Hippotigris) are African equines with distinctive black-and-white striped coats.
Located behind the nasal cavity where the nose meets the throat, which mass of lymphoid tissue is also known as the pharyngeal tonsil?
Adenoid: Type of tonsil. The adenoid, also known as the pharyngeal tonsil, or nasopharyngeal tonsil is the superior-most of the tonsils.

Born out of wedlock in the Caribbean and orphaned young, this Founding Father became the first U.S. secretary of the treasury and started America's first political party, the Federalist Party — who was he?
This memory disorder comes in two main forms — one blocking recall of events before a specific date, the other preventing new experiences from becoming lasting memories — what is it?
Amnesia: Cognitive disorder where memory is disturbed or lost.
Shed and regrown every year on most male deer, this bony head growth serves as both a weapon and a symbol of sexual attraction — what is it?
Antler: Skull projections found in deer.

A physician who began writing stories while studying medicine in Edinburgh, he was knighted in 1902 and created both a famous consulting detective and the dinosaur-filled adventure The Lost World. Who was he?
Arthur Conan Doyle: British writer and physician (1859–1930)
Nicknamed the hay bacterium for its soil habitat, this rod-shaped, spore-forming microbe is the best-studied Gram-positive species and a top industrial source of secreted enzymes — what is it?
Bacillus subtilis: Catalase-positive bacterium. It forms biofilms through the formation of extracellular polymeric matrix containing sugars and proteins.

This steel-gray, brittle alkaline earth metal is found naturally only in combination with other elements, making up gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, and bonds so strongly to oxygen that extracting it is notoriously difficult — which element, atomic number 4?
Beryllium: Chemical element with atomic number 4 (Be)

Announced at the 1984 Farnborough Airshow and launched by Northwest Airlines, this advanced wide-body airliner added 6-foot winglets and a stretched upper deck to an already-famous jumbo jet design — which aircraft?
Boeing 747-400: Wide-body airliner, improved production series of the 747.

Branching from the windpipe at a landmark called the carina, these airway passages narrow progressively through several orders before losing cartilage support and changing name entirely — what are they called?
Bronchus: Airway in the respiratory tract.
Which mammal family includes dromedaries, llamas, alpacas, and vicuñas among its seven living species?
Camelidae: Family of mammals. Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
Publishing a landmark 1912 paper on 'vital amines,' this Polish biochemist helped pioneer the concept now known as vitamins while researching pellagra and rickets — who is he?
Capable of sprinting up to 104 km/h, this spotted big cat is the fastest land animal alive, sporting black tear-like streaks down its face and a flexible spine built for speed — which animal?
Cheetah: Large feline of the genus Acinonyx.
Sold under the brand name Biaxin, this macrolide antibiotic treats everything from strep throat to H. pylori infections by slowing bacterial protein synthesis — what is it?
Clarithromycin: Antibiotic medication. Clarithromycin, sold under the brand name Biaxin among others, is an antibiotic used to treat various bacterial infections.
Blue above and orange below, this sparrow-sized bird dives for fish and nests in burrows dug into riverbanks — which species?
Common kingfisher: Species of bird. It is resident in much of its range, but migrates from areas where rivers freeze in winter.
Nicknamed the mosquito hawk, which long-legged insect of the superfamily Tipuloidea is often mistaken for an oversized mosquito?
Crane fly: Superfamily of flies. The larvae of crane flies are known commonly as leatherjackets.
First created in 1994 and named for the German city where it was made, this synthetic element sits below platinum in group 10 — what is it?
Darmstadtium: Chemical element with atomic number 110 (Ds)
Produced by the enzyme 5α-reductase acting on a more familiar male sex hormone, this compound is a more potent driver of prostate growth, sebum, and body hair — which hormone?
Sometimes called 'word blindness,' this learning disability makes it hard to spell, sound out words, and read quickly, and often co-occurs with ADHD — what is it?
The tallest and heaviest of all living penguins, this flightless Antarctic bird can top 45 kilograms and sports bright-yellow ear patches — which species is it?
Emperor penguin: Large flightless seabird endemic to Antarctica.
This Marine-turned-professor's 1981 memoir about fighting at Peleliu and Okinawa later inspired Ken Burns's The War and HBO's The Pacific, where he was played by Joseph Mazzello — who is he?
Made up mostly of undigested food broken down by gut bacteria, this bodily waste is expelled through the anus and can even be dried for fuel or used as fertilizer — what is it?
Feces: Solid or semisolid remains of undigested food.
Also called vitamin B9, this essential nutrient the body can't make itself is vital for building DNA and RNA — which is why its synthetic form, folic acid, is added to fortified foods. What is it?
Folate: Vitamin B9; nutrient essential for DNA synthesis. Folate, also known as vitamin B9 and folacin, is one of the B vitamins.
Also known as reishi or lingzhi, this red-colored fungus grows on decaying hardwood in parts of Europe and China — what is it?

This general term covers any organ that secretes substances either straight into the bloodstream, like endocrine ones, or through a duct to a body surface, like exocrine ones — what type of structure is it?
Gland: Type of animal organ. A gland may also function to remove unwanted substances such as urine from the body.
Known to the British as the Martlet, this American carrier-based fighter entered service in 1940 and remained the U.S. Navy's best fighter against the Mitsubishi Zero until mid-1943 — which aircraft?
Grumman F4F Wildcat: United States Navy World War II era fighter plane.
This German physicist was the first to conclusively demonstrate the electromagnetic waves predicted by James Clerk Maxwell's equations — who is he?
Introduced in 1948 by a French naturalist, this taxonomic tribe groups humans together with chimpanzees and bonobos, but excludes gorillas — which tribe?
Hominini: Tribe of mammals. The Hominini (hominins) form a taxonomic tribe of the subfamily Homininae (hominines).

When the thyroid gland churns out too much hormone, the result can be a racing heartbeat, heat intolerance, hand tremor and weight loss — and rarely, a life-threatening 'thyroid storm.' What is this condition?
Hyperthyroidism: Excessive production of thyroid hormone.

Marked by an IQ below 70 and deficits in everyday adaptive skills first apparent in childhood, this neurodevelopmental condition was formerly called 'mental retardation' in the U.S. — what is it now called?
Known as sampaguita in the Philippines, where it's the national flower, this fragrant vine or shrub also lends its blossoms to a beloved variety of tea — which species?
Jasminum sambac: Species of jasmine. Jasminum sambac (Arabian jasmine or Sambac jasmine or Mogra) is a species of jasmine native to Bhutan and India.
Also nicknamed the reed or swamp feline, this solitary wild predator ranges from the Caucasus to Southeast Asia and marks territory by urine spraying — which species?
This severe form of childhood protein malnutrition causes swelling and an enlarged, fatty liver, and is distinct from the calorie-deficient condition known as marasmus — what is it?
Kwashiorkor: Severe protein malnutrition. Kwashiorkor ( KWOSH-ee-OR-kor, -⁠kər) is a form of severe protein malnutrition characterized by edema and an enlarged liver with fatty infiltrates.
Often beginning in the bone marrow, this group of cancers floods the body with immature 'blast' cells, bringing easy bruising, bone pain, and frequent infections — what is it?
Predominantly black and white with pink and grey highlights, this small Eurasian bird forms social flocks of six to seventeen outside breeding season and often nests in thorny scrub. What is it?
Long-tailed tit: Species of bird in Europe and Asia.

Discovered in 2005 by the same Palomar team whose haul of big, icy Kuiper-belt bodies pushed astronomers to demote Pluto in 2006, this fourth-largest dwarf planet has a methane-frosted, tholin-reddened surface — what is it?
Makemake: Dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Powered by two rear-mounted engines under a T-tail and fitted with built-in airstairs, this twin-engine jetliner entered service with Delta Air Lines in December 1965 — which aircraft is it?
McDonnell Douglas DC-9: Jet airliner, produced 1965-1982.
Used to treat nausea, vomiting, and gastroparesis, this dopamine receptor antagonist is also prescribed for migraines and appears on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Metoclopramide: Medication. It is thus rarely recommended that people take the medication for longer than twelve weeks.
Its dust-like, colored, fuzzy appearance on food comes from spores, and its branching network of hyphae — called a mycelium — counts as a single organism; what fungal structure is this?
Mold: Wooly, dust-like fungal structure or substance.
This symbiotic partnership between fungus and plant roots plays a crucial role in plant nutrition and soil chemistry — usually mutualistic, but sometimes parasitic. What's the association called?
Mycorrhiza: Fungus-plant symbiotic association. The term mycorrhiza refers to the role of the fungus in the plant's rhizosphere, the plant root system and its surroundings.

This silvery-white transition metal with a faint golden tinge resists corrosion thanks to a thin oxide layer, and in pure native form it's mostly found inside iron meteorites — which element, atomic number 28, is it?
Nickel: Chemical element with atomic number 28 (Ni)
Known as holy basil and sacred within the Vaishnava tradition of Hinduism, which aromatic herb is widely used in Ayurvedic tea?
Ocimum tenuiflorum: Species of flowering plant.

Most members of this order of over 200 species are solitary night hunters with broad heads, binocular vision, and feathers tuned for silent flight — though oddballs like the burrowing kind break the mold. What are they?
Owl: Birds from the order Strigiformes.
This economist and longtime New York Times columnist was the sole winner of the 2008 Nobel for his work on new trade theory and economic geography. Who is he?
Found naturally in mammals' milk and a direct precursor to phenethylamine, this is one of nine amino acids your body can't make, so you eat it in meat, eggs, and legumes — which one?
This egg-laying Australian mammal hunts with its eyes, ears, and nostrils shut, sensing prey by electrolocation — and, oddly for a mammal, it's also venomous. What is it?
Platypus: Species of mammal. Like other monotremes, the platypus has a sense of electrolocation, which it uses to detect prey in water while its eyes, ears and nostrils are closed.
This New World family within the order Carnivora encompasses raccoons, ringtails, coatis, and kinkajous, most of them omnivorous — what family is it?
Procyonidae: Family of mammals. Procyonidae ( PROH-see-ON-i-dee) is a New World family of the order Carnivora.
Native to southern China, this pear tree's fruit goes by dozens of names worldwide - Asian pear, apple pear, nashi pear - but is rarely baked into pies due to its high water content - which species?
Pyrus pyrifolia: Species of pear with round crisp grainy fruit.
Rooted in Minangkabau cooking at the crossroads of the Malacca Strait, this dish slow-cooks meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — what is it?

Nicknamed the 'dark lady of DNA,' this X-ray crystallographer's crucial contributions to the discovery of DNA's structure went largely unrecognized in her lifetime — James Watson believed she'd have won a Nobel Prize had she lived. Who was she?
Also called Besnier–Boeck–Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition forms clusters of inflammatory cells called granulomata, often starting in the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis: Abnormal formation of clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomata)
Sold as Zoloft, this SSRI antidepressant treats major depression, OCD, panic disorder, and social anxiety, with common side effects like nausea and insomnia — what is it?
Sertraline: SSRI antidepressant. It should not be used together with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): this combination may cause serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening in some cases.
With the formula CH3COONa, this colorless, moisture-absorbing compound is the salt formed from acetic acid — what is it called?
A spherical, gram-positive bacterium that usually lives harmlessly on our skin and in our airways, this microbe can turn opportunistic and cause abscesses, sinusitis, and food poisoning — what is it?
Staphylococcus aureus: Species of Gram-positive bacterium. It is often positive for catalase and nitrate reduction and is a facultative anaerobe, meaning that it can grow without oxygen.
Native to Southern Europe and Anatolia, this deciduous tree produces an edible nut that's been used in cooking since ancient times — what is it commonly called?
Sweet chestnut: Species of tree. A substantial, long-lived deciduous tree, it produces an edible seed, the chestnut, which has been used in cooking since ancient times.
Famously nicknamed 'white ants,' these wood-munching eusocial insects are actually genetically closer to cockroaches than they are to true ants — what are they?
Termite: Social insects related to cockroaches.
He joined Apple in 1998 to run worldwide operations and stepped up to the top job in 2011 when Steve Jobs resigned — which executive now leads the company?

Endemic to New Zealand and often mistaken for a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that thrived back in the Mesozoic era — its Māori name means 'peaks on the back.' What is it?
Tuatara: Species of reptile. The tuatara (Māori: [ˈtʉ.a.ta.ɾa]; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.
This glycopeptide antibiotic is given intravenously for MRSA infections like endocarditis and meningitis, but taken orally - where it's poorly absorbed - to treat a common gut infection - which drug?
Vancomycin: Antibiotic medication. Vancomycin is also taken orally (by mouth) to treat Clostridioides difficile infections.
Recognized by their unusually long snouts, these small herbivorous beetles number around 97,000 species and include notorious crop pests that damage stored grain — what are they called?
Weevil: Superfamily of beetles. It also includes bark beetles, which while morphologically dissimilar to other weevils in lacking the distinctive snout, is a subfamily of Curculionidae.

Ranging from small shrubs to tree-like giants such as the Joshua tree, this North American desert plant genus relies on a specialized moth for pollination and is also called Adam's needle — what genus is it?
Yucca: Plant genus in the agave subfamily.

The symbol for iodine is I. Iodine is a chemical element; it has symbol I and atomic number 53.
